statement: Equation (1) presents the p-Wasserstein distance as an infimum over couplings between two probability distributions under a ground cost.
limits: A metric definition alone is not a MARL algorithm

statement: The paper proposes five OT-MARL application areas: policy alignment, resource management, non-stationarity, scalable learning, and energy efficiency.
Equations (2)-(3) propose minimizing pairwise Wasserstein distances between policy-induced distributions as a policy-alignment objective.
limits: Objective may collapse useful specialization if used naively

statement: Equations (6)-(8) propose measuring consecutive state-distribution shift with Wasserstein distance and mapping it to an adaptive policy learning rate.
conditions: Chosen mapping f from distance to learning rate
limits: No specified estimator, stability analysis, or experiment

statement: The challenges section identifies high-dimensional computational cost and repeated recalibration as obstacles, and suggests entropic approximation plus decentralized or hierarchical decomposition.
The paper contains no theorem, benchmark, sample size, or result showing that OT improves MARL performance, robustness, scalability, or held-out-N generalization.

A high-information HMASD test could compare a specified Wasserstein change observable or OT task allocator against a matched non-OT baseline under roster/distribution shifts, with compute cost included.
conditions: Fix ground cost, estimator, intervention, comparator, and resource budget
